Introduction to the workshop and a live demo of the project we build
toward — physics-informed inference of unknown drivers in a 1D vertical
ocean column with shallow-water coupling. Participants see the
destination on day one before working through the foundations.

::: {.callout-note}
This unit's demo is a stripped-down preview of
[Unit 8](../unit_08/unit_08.qmd) and
[Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd). Code in §1.2 will be assembled once
those units are finalised. The full model specification lives in
[Unit 10](../unit_10/unit_10.qmd).
:::

## 1.1 The AIMS Column Problem

### A Mooring Chain at a Reef Site

Imagine a thermistor chain moored in 100 m of water at a reef site
offshore from Townsville. Five sensors at depths 2, 10, 30, 60, and
90 m record temperature every hour for 30 days. After a storm passes
through, the deeper sensors record an unexpected cooling pattern. The
question — and the workshop project — is which physical mechanism
caused it.

### Vertical Heat Transport in One Picture

Heat enters the column from above (sun, atmosphere). Cold water can
be pushed up from below by currents elsewhere. Inside the column,
turbulent mixing redistributes heat vertically. The minimal model is
a 1D vertical advection–diffusion equation for temperature
$T(z, t)$ with surface and bottom boundary conditions — fully spelled
out in [Unit 10](../unit_10/unit_10.qmd).

### Three Storm Hypotheses

Three competing explanations for the observed cooling:

1. The storm intensified **upwelling** — cold water pumped up from depth.
2. The storm enhanced **vertical mixing** — heat drawn down from the surface faster than usual.
3. **Surface heating reduced** — cloud cover and evaporation cut the net flux into the ocean.

Each hypothesis leaves a distinct fingerprint in the depth–time
record. By Unit 9 we'll have a PINN that, given the mooring data,
can identify which mechanism dominated.

## 1.2 Live Demo

### Forward: Predicting the Column Response

Given the drivers — surface heat flux, upwelling profile, vertical
mixing — predict $T(z, t)$ across the 30-day window. We compare a
finite-difference reference solver against a forward PINN trained on
the same problem, both producing the diurnal warm layer riding on top
of a slowly evolving thermocline.

*Code placeholder — assembled from [Unit 8](../unit_08/unit_08.qmd).*

### Inverse: Recovering a Hidden Driver

Now hide one driver — say, the wind-stress envelope that controls
both upwelling and mixing — and try to recover it from the five
mooring time series alone. The PINN treats the unknown driver as a
small neural network trained jointly with the temperature field.

*Code placeholder — assembled from [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd).*

### Reading the Output

We plot the recovered driver against the synthetic ground truth and
compare predicted temperature traces against the noisy mooring
observations. The takeaway: PINNs do well at *inverse* problems with
sparse data — exactly the setting AIMS researchers face.

## 1.3 Course Roadmap

### What You'll Learn Across Units 2–8

[Unit 2](../unit_02/unit_02.qmd) cover machine-learning basics and
deep learning — the function-approximation toolkit. [Unit 3](../unit_03/unit_03.qmd)
surveys the broader Sci-ML and physics-informed ML landscape.
[Unit 4](../unit_04/unit_04.qmd) introduces ODEs through universal
approximation (Neural ODEs, UDEs). [Unit 5](../unit_05/unit_05.qmd)
is your first PINN, on basic ODE and PDE models.
[Unit 6](../unit_06/unit_06.qmd) covers formal PDE theory and
classical numerics. [Unit 7](../unit_07/unit_07.qmd) covers modern
PINN techniques for harder PDEs.

### Returning to This Demo in Units 8–9

[Unit 8](../unit_08/unit_08.qmd) builds the full forward column +
shallow-water model. [Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) closes the loop
by recovering an unknown driver from sparse mooring data — exactly
the demo above, fully derived.

### 75% Julia, 25% Python

Julia is the primary language: `Lux.jl`, `NeuralPDE.jl`,
`MethodOfLines.jl`, the broader SciML stack. Python parallels appear
in Unit 2 (`scikit-learn` and `PyTorch`), and Unit 9
(`DeepXDE`) so participants leave with a sense of the cross-ecosystem
landscape.
